utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-42-PT, the Prosecutor versus Miodrag Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: May we have the appearances please. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Susan L. Somers, lead counsel for the Prosecution. To my right, extreme right, Mr. John Cencich of the investigative team; Mr. Massimo Scaliotti, a trial partner; and Mr. Vladimir Tochilovsky, also a trial lawyer; Ms. Susan Grogan, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Alun Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I turn to the representative from the government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm Vladan Batic, Justice Minister in the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. This hearing is for the provisional release for Mr. Jokic. This Trial Chamber has been seized of these two motions. One is the motion for the provisional release for Mr. Jokic filed on 18th December 2001. Another one is the Prosecution's filing, that is, the response to the motion for the provisional release of Mr. Jokic. First of all, we would like to hear from the Defence counsel about their views concerning this very matter. We have received your motion already. I guess all of us have already read the contents. I hope in a few minutes you could sum up the main contents of your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. My application, or my motion, is a short and simple one. Your Honours, as the Court knows, Admiral Jokic, who is a retired vice-admiral of the Yugoslav navy, he voluntarily presented himself to the Tribunal on the 12th of November of 2001. He did that of his own free will. He is a married man who lives in Belgrade with his wife and one of their two children. It is my submission to the Tribunal that he is entitled, as of right, to provisional release under Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Your Honours, I place weight on the following facts: that under Rule 65(B), release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only after hearing the host country and only if it is satisfied the accused will appear for trial and, if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or other person. Your Honours, the Court can be, and can only be, in my submission, satisfied that those conditions are met, because there is no material presented to the contrary by the Prosecutor. It is not suggested by the Prosecutors or by their investigators that there are any such grounds to believe that Admiral Jokic will not appear for trial, nor is it suggested that he will pose any danger to any victim, witness, or other person. Your Honours, I do wish to submit that in those circumstances, particularly since the deletion of the words "in exceptional circumstances" in December of 1999, I do respectfully submit that he is entitled, bearing in mind the presumption of innocence, as of right, to bail, to provisional release, in those circumstances, conditioned, of course, by the elementary and, I hope, uncontroversial guarantees which he has signed and indeed are accepted by the government of the Republic of Serbia. Now, Your Honours, having said that, the terms of provisional release have, of course, subject to the views of the Tribunal, been the subject of agreement between Prosecution and Defence in the terms in which they're proposed in the motion at Annex A and B. And in particular, Admiral Jokic will not leave the territory of Serbia and will reside at the addresses which have been disclosed to the Tribunal. He freely gives his consent to the Ministry of the Interior to make checks to ensure that he remains at his home; he will report every day to the said ministry; will not communicate with his co-accused; he won't discuss the case with anyone, including the media, except his lawyers; and that he'll return to the Tribunal at the times requested by the Tribunal. So it may be (H) has been somewhat overtaken by events. The defendant will return to the Netherlands to be interviewed, when requested, on reasonable notice by representatives of the Prosecution, and he'll comply with any altered or amended conditions of provisional release. Now, Your Honours, there have been difficulties since November in arranging for interviews. It has been Admiral Jokic's position, from the time he arrived, that he wishes to put forward his side of events to the Prosecutor, but it hasn't been possible or practicable, for reasons I hope it will be unnecessary to go into, to arrange for those four days to be done. But Your Honour, without in any way prejudicing my submission that he is entitled, as of right, to provisional release, I should tell the Court, for the purposes of orderly case management, that he appreciates that it's in everybody's interests that he gives his side of events to the Prosecutor early rather than late, and I can tell the Tribunal that if he's given provisional release - or even if he isn't given provisional release - there is no reason that we can see why he should not be interviewed by the Prosecutor's investigators within the period of the next three weeks. Now, if I develop myself further, I'm afraid I shall be repeating myself, but those are the terms on which I respectfully ask the Court to grant provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that Judge Orie will have some questions to address to you on these particular issues since he is the Presiding Judge -- I'm sorry, the Pre-Trial Judge on this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have a few questions to you. Let me limit myself to three questions. You indicated that Rule 65(B), as of right, should guide the Chamber in granting bail, as you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rule 65(B) doesn't read that the release shall be ordered by a Trial Chamber after hearing the host country, if it is satisfied, et cetera. It says the release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only after hearing the host country and only if it is satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I'd like, especially when I look at the case law of this Tribunal, the words that "as of right" an accused is entitled to bail, if the two requirements are satisfied, might be quicker spoken and explained. That's my first question to you. Second question is: It seems to me if we look at what kind of conditions have been put in the context of provisional release, that you picked out a few, and as far as I understand, you agree on these conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I could imagine that, without giving any idea, without giving any position as what the decision of this Chamber will be, of course, that there might be some other ones as well, and I'd like you to consider whether, for example, a decision that there would be no contact with any co-accused, I don't think that that's one of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think it is at one, at Annex A, letter D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. Yes, yes, of course. Well, my question is: Is this the single or the plural?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Plural. It is intended to be plural, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's no question any more, so it's valid for all co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then one of the conditions that have been imposed by one of the Trial Chambers in this Tribunal is that the accused would not occupy any official position in the relevant country. Would that be an acceptable condition, apart from the general rule that any amendment would be acceptable, but I'd just like to raise this specific condition which has been imposed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I would like to formally speak to Admiral Jokic about this, but if it's acceptable to the Court I could do that immediately now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you could ask Mr. Jokic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My last question would be, in any motion, apart from giving assurances by General Jokic, you also rely on assurances given or to be given by the -- or partly already been given by the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The assurances given by the Republic of Serbia, as far as I can read them, is that the government is aware of the obligations undertaken by Admiral Jokic, and it will take all necessary action through its competent authorities to ensure that, and then the whole list comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the assurances is that he will return to the ICTY at times requested by the ICTY. This would ultimately have to result, if, of course - which I do not expect at this moment but you never know what will happen in the future - but if Admiral Jokic would decide not to return voluntarily to the Tribunal, this ultimately would result in an arrest and sending him back, at least if that is a necessary action. I think it would be. The question is whether there are any competent authorities, whether there is any legislation in force, to ultimately arrest Admiral Jokic and to send him back to the Tribunal. What would be the legal basis for that, since I do understand that there is some discussion in the Republic of Serbia on the legal basis of arrests and rendering people to the Tribunal. So I'd like to know what in your view, since you're relying on these assurances of the government as well, what would be the legal basis for this ultimate consequence of their undertakings?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour, I just cannot immediately answer that without taking instructions. Your Honour, I wonder if I might perhaps deal with the first of the question that was put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if the presiding -- Mr. President, you agree that -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn to this matter later also, I think, with the representatives of the government, but since you're relying on it, I first ask you, and of course at a later stage similar questions might be put to the representative of the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honours. If I could deal with the first question, this does, in my submission, pose a very interesting juridical question. The reason I made the submissions that I did about the meaning of Rule 65(B) is that I submit it's very difficult to think of any circumstances in which, if the Court were satisfied that the person before it was obviously prepared to come back to the court, and if he was perfectly peaceful and peaceable, it's very difficult in my submission to envisage any circumstances in which the Court would say, "We appreciate that there is a presumption of innocence, we appreciate this man will come back, and he's behaved honourably and come here, but nonetheless, we are going to refuse an application for provisional release." And the reason I've expressed myself as I have is because one is very anxious to cope for all possible considerations that the Prosecution might wish to raise, which is why I expressed it in the way I did in our motion for provisional release, and that the Court may raise, because a person in Admiral Jokic's position, or a person contemplating being in his position, is surely entitled, in my respectful submission, to some certainty that he does have a right, if he's behaved honourably, if he's surrendered himself to the jurisdiction of the court, if he's a person of good character as envisaged by Rule 65, and it is my submission that that construction is consistent with the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly Article 5, which we cite in the motion. And it's because that we are very -- I am very anxious upon his behalf to ensure that provisional release, so far as I can, is granted, that I do wish to rest upon that legal foundation, and as well as the other factual circumstances. And in my respectful submission, the Tribunal might think it appropriate to approach it in that way rather than as a matter of grace towards people who are of good character. Now, it might be in the end, Your Honours, that the decision of the Tribunal in this case, or the Chamber in this case, will not depend upon that construction, but if the Tribunal were minded to say -- to consider that provisional release should not be granted upon those conditions, then, in my respectful submission, it would be right for the Tribunal to grapple with this question in -- and to articulate in legal terms the basis upon which, now that the words "in exceptional circumstances" have been deleted, the circumstances in which a Tribunal might simply, of its own discretion, refuse, even where none of those conditions applied. That's the way I put it, and I hope I'm not putting it in a way which in any way appears to the Tribunal as offensive. But when a person in his position comes voluntarily towards this Tribunal, there are no considerations of that sort, I do argue that the Tribunal ought to say, "We respect that. Yes. You are entitled. We accept that you will come back and you are entitled to provisional release." Now, Your Honour, that is the way I put it on the matter, and if I rightly sense that Mr. Batic, as the Minister of Justice, is in a position to deal with the third of your questions, then, in my respectful submission, since it's a matter of Serbian law, it might be more appropriate for the Tribunal to hear on that matter from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- I think the order was that -

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: - but, Mr. President, you'll take over - the Prosecution would then have an opportunity now to -- well, not to respond, but to explain their position and perhaps keep in mind already some of the questions that I put to the Defence, and then of course we'll then Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. continue with the representatives of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. The Prosecution does not view Rule 65 as seeing the actual release as a matter of right, but the application, the ability to apply, is a right guaranteed. Again, I concur -- the Prosecution totally concurs with Your Honour's reading of the "may," the permissive language, and this is just on purely the legal point. It is not necessarily going to today's hearing, because there are factors. We have stated our position in writing. But on the actual legal question, we wholeheartedly concur that it is not a matter of right to receive it. It has to be assessed, and it is a matter within the sound discretion of the Chamber to rule upon. Having said that, in this particular instance, the presence of the distinguished representatives across from me to offer the assurances which are required should, hopefully, make -- or provide to the Chamber the necessary assurance about appearance and about the activities when in a jurisdiction outside the physical reach of this Tribunal. Again, the distinction between this Tribunal and a domestic jurisdiction is our ability, physically, to enforce anything outside our own very limited physical territory. Again, having said that, the representations that I anticipate will be made and have been initially discussed should satisfy this Chamber. I regret that Ms. Del Ponte herself was unable to appear. She would have liked to. But the one issue which we have discussed - and I am very grateful to my learned counsel opposite for raising - is the willingness and the ability to submit to an interview, and it is the Prosecution's position that its non-opposition, simply its non-opposition, viewed that as a very important point, very critical to our actually putting in writing our position, and it is good to hear that this matter should be taken care of within three or so weeks. We have had the opportunity to meet with Mr. Jones just before this hearing. We discussed some of these matters, which is helpful. And we will do everything within our power to facilitate the orderly execution of this particular process, which is, of course, very important to our position. Beyond that, Your Honours, we have stated everything. I think that there is nothing further I can add. It is regrettable that we were unable to accomplish it before leaving, for judicial economy, and I believe as was contemplated by the Prosecution. That opportunity is behind us, unfortunately, and now we look forward to taking care of it as expeditiously as possible. If I may be of any further assistance to any inquiries on the essential grounds for release, please may I ask you to inquire of me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'd like to address the representative of the government of the Republic of Serbia. Mr. Batic, I was informed that you're accompanied by a representative of the government of the Federation of Yugoslavia. Is my understanding right that as far as fulfilling whatever conditions is concerned, that it's the Republic of Serbia who is making the undertakings?

utterances.speaker: MR. BATIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Of course, you're entirely free to stand up if you want to, but ... I have a few -- one of the questions I raised in respect of fulfilling the conditions was whether the legal framework was there in order to effectively make assurances at this moment. Perhaps you could first inform the Chamber about that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The government of the Republic of Serbia has reached a decision on the 15th of November last year to provide guarantees for the provisional release of Admiral Jokic. As Minister of Justice in the government of the Republic of Serbia, I wished to confirm these guarantees here in person, which have been presented in Annex B in written form. In response to your question, I would like to inform you that the government of the Republic of Serbia, on the 28th of June, 2001, reached a decision about the automatic application of the Statute of The Hague Tribunal. This decision was published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, and on the basis of that decision, in the case of Slobodan Milosevic, he was extradited, and also the brothers Banovic were extradited as well under that decision. So this is the legal basis upon which the government of the Republic of Serbia is cooperating with The Hague Tribunal, which, in the specific reply to your question, means that the government of the Republic of Serbia is obliged, in case the request by Admiral Jokic is refused -- in case Admiral Jokic refuses to comply with the summons of the International Tribunal. So the government of Serbia is then, in that case, obliged to arrest him and transfer Admiral Jokic to the International Tribunal. This would be much easier, because Admiral Jokic will have absolute and permanent 24-hour monitoring by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, both as a guarantee of his own security and in order to comply with all the obligations contained in the written guarantees of the Republic of Serbia, the government of the Republic of Serbia. If you permit me, I would like to say something else. In the identical way, the government of the Republic of Serbia provided guarantees in the case of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic. Of course, I do not wish to make any parallels between these two cases, but I do wish to say that the government of the Republic of Serbia, by providing guarantees, places its international legal credibility, as well as its dignity in general, at a risk, and it would like very much to keep and to preserve this international credibility which has been quite hard to earn. So we have provided guarantees only in two cases so far: for Biljana Plavsic, which guarantees the Trial Chamber accepted. She is currently in Belgrade and is complying with all the conditions contained in the guarantee, which means that the case of Admiral Jokic would not be an isolated precedent. Having in mind the fact that we have also taken into consideration his moral character as well as his own personal guarantees, I would also like to respond to your third question, if you permit me, which you directed to the Defence counsel, Mr. Jones. Admiral Jokic is not able to perform any official duties because he's retired. He's in retirement, and under the laws of the Republic of Serbia, since he happens to be a retired person, cannot perform any other professional or official duties. I am prepared also to answer to any other questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that in the conditions that have been proposed by the Defence and agreed upon by the Prosecution that I don't think that there's any obligation to regularly report to the Tribunal about the fulfilment of the conditions, at least if I -- I see that you'll do everything -- that Admiral Jokic would be under an obligation to report to the authorities, but unlike in some other cases, where the Chamber has requested the government to report to the Tribunal on a regular basis. That's what is missing, at least in the proposed conditions, and I wondered whether the government would be prepared to report on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. We have done this in the case of Mrs. Plavsic, and this is something which is carried out by the Ministry of Justice. I have signed the guarantees for Admiral Jokic on behalf of the government, so I would like to state that in the intervals that the Tribunal requests, we will regularly keep the Tribunal informed about the status of Admiral Jokic. So these guarantees absolutely stand, because I, as Minister of Justice, feel that it is my duty to keep the Tribunal informed and to abide by all the agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For me it was just a matter of clarification, because it's not explicit in the conditions. But I do understand. And by your answer, I do understand that one of the other conditions that is regularly put in these kinds of situations is to provide personal security and safety. You told this already, that this is also part of your undertaking as you perceive it. Perhaps one final question: You say that it's a matter of the government to decide to cooperate with the Tribunal. You told us that the automatic application of the Statute was prevailing above any national legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is the government's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, you will be aware -- and I'm not putting any question to you on it, but I'll give you an opportunity if you want to express yourself on that issue. We have seen over the last period of time both that people were detained and were transferred to the Tribunal. We also have seen that some people accused by the Prosecution were not detained and were not transferred to the Tribunal. You'll understand that this might raise some questions in the Tribunal as well. I'm not putting a specific answer to you; I'm just telling you that it's my observation that this happens, and if you find there's any reason to express yourself, then of course the opportunity is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has nothing to do directly with the questions that we are discussing, but I think that you are familiar with the circumstances prevailing in the Yugoslav Federation regarding cooperation with The Hague Tribunal and also are familiar with the degree of political controversy. I am speaking on behalf of the government of the Republic of Serbia, which has reached a decision, because unfortunately, at the federal level, the law on cooperation with the Tribunal has not as yet been adopted, so the Republic of Serbia, based on its constitution, decided to automatically apply the Statute of the Hague Tribunal. Perhaps the Tribunal is not satisfied with the pace of the transfers, but I can claim responsibly that the government of the Republic of Serbia wishes to be cooperative and wishes for intensive cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, but at the same time, I would like to say that this cooperation should sometimes go both ways. This example, and also the proceedings against Admiral Jokic, can confirm this two-way cooperation in the best possible way, because we believe that people who surrender voluntarily, who provide guarantees on their own, and who the government trusts so that the government provides guarantees on their behalf, should have certain benefits in proceedings before this Honourable Tribunal. There is an analogy here relating to national legal systems. I think that this would also be a positive factor regarding the factor of public opinion in Serbia, which would contribute to an intensification of cooperation, as well as to the motivation of some people to also surrender voluntarily to The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for -- that you have taken the opportunity to make some observation on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: May I ask you a question, Mr. Batic? Can I ask you a question? Well, first of all, I would like to say that we are extremely grateful for your appearance before this Tribunal on this very short notice, and appreciate very much your willingness to come here, to cooperate with this Tribunal. My question is that I wonder whether you could shed some light on the relationship between the federal government and the Republic of Serbia. Could the federal government interfere into the guarantees which will be made by your government concerning the accused's provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MR. BATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, the answer is no. On the territory of the Republic of Serbia, it is the government of the Republic of Serbia that has exclusive jurisdiction - namely the Ministry of the Interior, the powers of the Ministry of Justice - in terms of all the powers that are involved in this specific case, namely in the case of the accused, Admiral Jokic. I'm trying to say that the federal government and the federal state have some other authorities, some other powers, but as far as this particular authority is concerned, for providing these guarantees, this is only enjoyed by the Republic of Serbia and its government, and that is why I am present here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Jokic, do you have anything to say on this very issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I do have something to say. The events due to which I have been indicted occurred 11 years ago. The Office of the Prosecutor had several years to investigate all the allegations made in witness statements, everything that is contained in documents, et cetera. The possibilities of the Defence are truly modest in this situation, when I am detained and when I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was not in a position, until now, to set up my own Defence team. I think, if I may put it this way as I address you, that for the sake of justice and fairness, I should also be given the possibility to prepare my defence in better circumstances than the current ones. Right now, I'm really not in a position to do so. At the time of the indictment, I did not know that this would actually take place. The indictment was sealed and I really had no possibility then - I have been a retired person for the past ten years now - to prepare myself. Therefore, my request is the following: I voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal, and as far as I am concerned, I believe there is no reason why I should not be allowed to prepare my defence, namely to be provisionally released. When the Honourable Court deems it necessary to call me, I shall certainly come and report here. If you have any other questions to address to me, I stand ready to answer them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have heard the submissions from both parties. We also heard the views expressed by the representative of the government of Serbia. We will take notice of the views expressed by the accused himself, and this Trial Chamber will make its decision concerning this matter at a later stage. I believe that is all on our agenda, so we will rise.
